decision: A company's interview loop is packaged as a season with one episode per round, the series pattern popularized by video-streaming apps
why: People binge a season in order; a loop has an order too, and seeing it as episodes makes preparation feel finishable.
alternative: A wiki page of interview notes.
value: Members prepare round by round, in the order they'll face them.

decision: An 'next episode in 8' countdown starts episode 3 on the shared now-playing bar, with 'Practice episode 3 first' and 'Stay here' as equal choices; reduced motion skips the countdown
why: Autoplay keeps momentum, but the best next step is sometimes practice, not more watching; both must be one click.
value: Momentum without trapping anyone in passive watching.

decision: Episodes are built from member reports (14 this season, a new one arriving live), and each shows its pass rate and what was asked
why: Credibility comes from provenance: people trust 'built from 14 reports' more than an anonymous guide.
value: Every claim in an episode traces back to members who sat the loop.

decision: A loop that isn't complete shows the missing episodes as dashed placeholders with what they need (two more reports) and a Notify me toggle
why: Hiding incomplete loops hides useful partial knowledge; showing gaps honestly also asks members to contribute.
value: Partial loops help sooner, and the gap is a call for reports.

decision: 'Members who passed' and the median offer are aggregated per company and season, never per person, and appear only above a minimum count
why: Small groups can be re-identified; aggregation thresholds keep outcome data useful without exposing anyone.
value: Useful benchmarks with privacy by construction.
